subject: Peak-shape discovery: latency bands, concurrency, and token burst profile
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
To: Kyle Baxter <kyle@shipmate.com>
Cc: neha_kapoor@redwood.com, jordan_blake@redwood.com
Date: Mon, 22 Jun 2026 15:08:00 -0700
Subject: Peak-shape discovery: latency bands, concurrency, and token burst profile

Hey Kyle — thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap and a few asks so we can scope a pilot correctly. I put Neha and Jordan on copy for ops/throughput planning.

Key notes we captured on the call:
- Traffic shape: you described a large number of short interactive sessions (2–6 turns), plus a small percentage (~4%) of long-running streams for transcription/real-time summarization.
- Peak behavior: crest-overflow pattern — very short, high-intensity crests lasting 20–60s that can repeat several times per minute during checkout surges.
- Basal (sustained) load: ~120 QPS baseline (1–2k tokens/s), peaks up to ~1.8k QPS observed in the last spike (customer telemetry).
- Latency goals: p95 end-to-end target 250ms for single-turn interactive calls; p99 target <= 450ms. Streaming segments can tolerate higher per-chunk latency but need steady throughput for KV-cache reuse.
- Concurrency: user sessions average 1.2 concurrent model streams per user, but your spike tests pushed that to 8–12 simultaneous streams from a single region.

Immediate asks (sorted):
1) Could you share the traffic sample CSV you mentioned in the call (schema: timestamp, user_id, request_type, tokens_in, tokens_out, duration_ms)? We can ingest and run a tokenization + crest analysis.
2) Confirm whether the long-running streams are full audio transcripts (avg chunk size 1.5–2k tokens) or micro-chunks (200–500 tokens). That changes our batching/KV strategy.
3) Any hard concurrency limits from your side (per-region egress, connection pools)?

Proposed next steps from Redwood:
- Neha will run a crest vs basal decomposition of your sample and return a tokens/sec heatmap + recommended slot sizing.
- Jordan will map the latency band targets to model variants and streaming chunk sizes; he will include fallback model suggestions for graceful degradation during extreme crests.
- If you can share the CSV by EOD tomorrow, we’ll prioritize a short analysis and propose a pilot capacity plan by Thu.

Attachments: please attach the traffic sample file. I’m attaching a quick worksheet we’ll use to map p95/p99 bands to QPS and tokens/sec (redwood_latency_matrix.xlsx).

Thanks — talk soon.

—

From: Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.com>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>, Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.com>
Cc: Kyle Baxter <kyle@shipmate.com>
Date: Tue, 23 Jun 2026 13:27:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Peak-shape discovery: latency bands, concurrency, and token burst profile

Thanks Kyle — I pulled the CSV and did a first-pass crest decomposition (attached short notes). Early observations:
- The crest windows are very spiky (median crest length ~28s) with inter-crest gaps often <45s during promos. This suggests we should avoid long batching windows for crest traffic; instead use aggressive multiplexing + small-batch sampling to keep client p95 under 250ms.
- Token mix: crest windows have a higher mean token-per-request (1.1k) than basal windows (420). That drives up per-token cost during crests and increases memory pressure on KV caches.
- Streaming guidance: for TRANSCRIBE_LONG we recommend chunking to ~1k tokens/chunk on the client when possible; that preserves KV reuse and reduces per-chunk decoding overhead.

Open questions for sizing:
1) For the pilot, do you want us to target sustained SLOs for basal traffic only and run crest mitigation as an overlay, or do you want a single configuration tuned to handle both simultaneously? (We can size dedicated slots vs. ephemeral burst capacity.)
2) Can you confirm whether your websocket pool will multiplex >1 logical session per connection? That changes how we think about concurrency counts per connection.

Next actions: I’ll produce a short pilot slot recommendation (CSV + notes) and mark expected cost delta for crest-capacity vs. single-config approach. Jordan — can you weigh in on fallback model choices and streaming chunk thresholds, then I’ll finalize the matrix.

—
Neha Kapoor
Principal Performance Engineer, Redwood Inference

From: Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.com>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>, Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.com>, Kyle Baxter <kyle@shipmate.com>
Date: Wed, 24 Jun 2026 11:42:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Peak-shape discovery: latency bands, concurrency, and token burst profile

Kyle / Team — quick follow and proposed pilot plan:

Short answers to Neha’s open questions:
- Pilot configuration: split approach recommended. 1) Basal dedicated slot(s) sized for the steady ~120 QPS (optimizing for cost). 2) Ephemeral burst pool (pre-warmed) reserved to absorb 80–90% of crest load; fallback policy to a smaller-vocab model if crest > burst capacity. This keeps the p95 goal for interactive paths and provides graceful degradation.
- Websocket multiplexing: if you can enable 2–3 logical sessions per connection we can reduce connection overhead and provision fewer upstream slots — that’s a moderate engineering change on your side but high ROI.

Pilot test plan (proposal):
1) Redwood runs an ingest of the CSV and returns: crest heatmap, tokens/sec timeline, recommended slot counts (basal + burst), and cost delta. (Deliverable: redwood_latency_matrix.xlsx + a short runbook) — timeline: 48 hours after we receive final CSV (we already have the trimmed file).
2) 2-hour smoke test with 70% crest replication (we’ll synthetic-run crest patterns against a staging endpoint with your team) to validate fallback behavior and p99 stability.
3) If smoke looks good, we run a one-day pilot window with live traffic routing (can be gradual, e.g., 5% -> 25% -> 50%).

Can we schedule the smoke test for this coming Friday morning PST? Kyle — please confirm availability and whether your team can enable 2x multiplexing on the websocket pool for the test.

Thanks — I’ll attach the pilot mapping notes and a sample runbook in the next update.

—
Jordan Blake
Performance PM, Redwood Inference
jordan_blake@redwood.com
